t: Introduction: the place of poisoning in forensic medicine
n: In this lecture we will consider the place of poisoning in forensic medicine. Impairment of health and deaths under the action of chemical factors are relatively common in forensic medical examination of corpses and living persons. Among violent deaths, poisonings take third place after mechanical injuries and mechanical asphyxia. The formation of forensic medicine as a science began precisely with forensic toxicology. Forensic toxicology solves the tasks set by law enforcement agencies in cases of poisoning.

t: The concepts of poison and poisoning
n: The concepts of poison and poisoning. Poison is a relative concept: a substance a small amount of which impairs health or leads to death. There is neither an absolute poison nor an absolutely harmless substance. According to Paracelsus, only the dose makes a given substance a medicine or a poison. Toxicology studies poisons and poisoning: there are industrial, agricultural, military, food, domestic and forensic branches. Attention: the other types of toxicology are directed at causes, aid and prevention; forensic toxicology solves legal tasks.

We consider how poisonings may arise. Iatrogenic poisoning is accidental and is related to an error in determining the dose of a drug during a medical procedure. An iatrogenic situation is also seen when another substance is mistakenly used instead of one drug. In an accident, poisoning occurs by chance and makes up the majority of cases. Suicide is deliberate and stands in second place. Homicide is also deliberate, but occurs in rare cases. Attention: in homicide and suicide, poisoning occurs deliberately, whereas in an accident it occurs by chance.

t: Four groups of factors affecting poisoning
n: In poisoning four groups of factors are significant: the poison, the organism, the route of entry and external conditions. They are considered one after another, like a chain. The faster and more completely the poison passes into the blood, the stronger the toxic action. External conditions are important only for certain substances: with alcohol and carbon monoxide, a closed, warm, humid environment increases the danger. That is, each factor must be assessed separately, since their importance is not the same for every substance.

We look at factors related to the poison. The chemical structure of a substance determines its properties: carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide have similar structures, but their toxicity is not the same. Dose and concentration are important: the action of a 3% solution of acetic acid cannot be compared with that of acetic essence. A gas acts more strongly than a liquid, and a liquid more strongly than a solid, because it passes into the blood faster. Barium sulphate is insoluble, while barium chloride is soluble and a strong poison. The vehiculum, that is the medium carrying the poison in, alters the action: arsenic is intensified in an alkaline medium, whereas cyanides act more strongly in an acid medium.

Factors related to the organism. Body weight: the same amount does not act in the same way on people of different weights, which is why a drug dose is calculated per kilogram of weight. Age is also important: children are more sensitive than adults, because their weight is small and the general system of resistance is not fully formed. Health: a healthy organism resists more strongly; in diseases of the heart, liver and kidneys this ability is limited. Genetics also plays a role: congenitally low cholinesterase activity enhances the action of muscle relaxants. Hypersensitivity to some substances is called idiosyncrasy.

Tolerance, dependence and abstinence. If a poison acts repeatedly over a short time, the organism may become habituated to it. This state is called tolerance. In medical practice tolerance is seen when taking sleeping drugs, analgesics and hypotensive, that is blood-pressure-lowering, preparations. With narcotic substances, mental and physical dependence forms together with tolerance. For this reason a drive appears to take the substance again and in larger amounts. Mental dependence is an irresistible drive. Physical dependence is the need to raise the dose because of tolerance.

t: Route of entry of the poison and external conditions
n: Route of entry of the poison and external conditions. A poison may enter through the skin, mouth, respiratory tract, rectum or by injection. The faster and more completely it passes into the blood, the stronger its action. Substances insoluble in both water and fat can act only locally. Substances readily soluble in fat, for example organophosphorus compounds, are absorbed even through healthy skin. Substances absorbed from the mucosa of the respiratory tract, rectum and vagina do not pass through the liver. Therefore they act more strongly than those absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract.

Case analysis. A faulty stove was burning in a closed, warm, humid room. In the room, a person with liver disease drank alcohol, fell asleep, and was found dead in the morning. External factor: a closed, warm, humid environment predisposes to poisoning with alcohol and carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide enters through the respiratory tract. Organism factor: in diseases of the liver, heart and kidneys, the organism's ability to resist poison is considerably limited. Question: name the factors of poison, organism and external conditions that raised the risk of poisoning in this situation. Which route of entry is significant?

t: The three stages of forensic medical diagnosis
n: The three stages of forensic medical diagnosis. The diagnosis of poisoning relies on data collected in three stages. First stage: examination of the scene or the place where the corpse was found with a specialist, and study of medical documents. Second stage: examination of the corpse. Third stage: poisoning is confirmed by additional laboratory examinations. At the end, the expert's report is drawn up.

The scene and medical documents. In examining the scene, attention is paid to the surroundings, foreign odour, drug containers, packaging, used syringes and prescriptions. The presence of secretions and vomit at the scene is recorded. The relevant physical evidence is collected for the laboratory. The first stage also includes becoming familiar with the case materials, the follow-up history and medical documents. With poisons that proceed with functional changes, the clinical description and the laboratory results from the medical institution may be weighty evidence.

t: External signs on the corpse: colour and odour
n: External signs on the corpse: colour and odour. In carbon monoxide, cadaveric lividity is pink. In cyanides, the lividity is bright cherry and a bitter almond smell is noticed. With methaemoglobin-forming poisons the lividity is brown. In acetic acid a sharp odour comes from the internal organs. With substances causing haemolysis, cadaveric lividity is yellowish. Rigor mortis in strychnine is rapid and strong; in chloral hydrate, curare and muscle relaxants it is weak and slack. In many functional poisons there may be no characteristic changes on external and internal examination.

t: Laboratory examination and the "three points" rule
n: Laboratory examination and the "three points" rule. Of the laboratory examinations, forensic chemical, that is toxicological, examination is carried out most often. It must determine both quality and quantity. If the poison is known, the "three points" rule is applied: samples are taken from the place where the poison entered, where it mainly acted, and where it left. If the poison is unknown: 1/3 of the brain, 1/4 of the lung, 1/3 of the liver with bile, a kidney, stomach contents, intestine and 100–200 ml of blood are taken. In deep putrefaction, 1.5–2.0 kg of mass from a mixture of chest and abdominal organs, that is an "average sample", is taken.

Toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics. Toxicokinetics is the change in the quantity and quality of the poison: entry, distribution, metabolism, elimination. Biotransformation occurs mainly in the liver; if organophosphorus compounds are oxidised, their toxicity is enhanced. The action may be primary, subsequent or metatoxic. An example of metatoxic action is acetic acid: burn, haemolysis, toxic hepatitis and nephrosis.

t: Case analysis: methanol and its metabolite
n: Case analysis: methanol. Methyl alcohol has been drunk instead of ethyl alcohol, because their colour, smell and taste are similar. The lethal dose is 30–100 ml. At first there is weak, brief intoxication and sleep. Then a latent stage: the condition improves, and it lasts from a few hours to several days. Methanol is slowly oxidised, forming formaldehyde and formic acid. Acidosis, visual disturbance and, after 2–3 days, paralysis of the respiratory centre develop. Question: why does the patient remain in danger even during the period of improvement, and which substance is strongly poisonous?

Forensic medical classification of poisons. Poisons are divided into two: those acting mainly locally and those acting mainly generally, that is resorptively. Local poisons include acids, alkalis and tincture of iodine; necrosis occurs at the site of contact. A resorptive poison acts after absorption into the blood. It is divided into destructive, blood and functional groups. Destructive poisons include mercury, lead, arsenic and phosphorus. Haemotropic poisons, for example carbon monoxide, act on the properties of blood. Functional poisons disturb the work of the central and peripheral nervous system; these include cyanide, alcohol, strychnine and opiates. Classification after V. L. Popov, 1990.

Corrosive substances: acids. In forensic practice, poisoning with acetic acid is common, most often as a method of suicide. Other acids are less common, usually in accidents. The free hydrogen ions of the acid dehydrate tissue and coagulate protein. As a result coagulative, that is dry, necrosis and a dense, dry brown-black scab form. Lethal dose in concentrated form: sulphuric and nitric 5–10 ml, hydrochloric 15–20 ml, acetic essence at 40–80% 20–40 ml, carbolic acid 10–30 ml.

Alkalis and other corrosive substances. Attention: an acid causes dry, that is coagulative, necrosis, whereas an alkali causes soft, slippery, that is colliquative, necrosis. The lethal dose of potassium and sodium hydroxide is 10–15 g, and of ammonium hydroxide, that is ammonia solution, 25–40 ml. The local action of ammonium hydroxide is weaker. If absorbed into the blood, the work of the respiratory centre may be disturbed. Formalin 37–40% fixes the mucosa and gives a characteristic smell in the internal organs. With potassium permanganate there is a brownish-reddish scab, and 15–20 g lead to death. Of hydrogen peroxide, 100 ml of 33% perhydrol may cause death. With iodine preparations there is a brown scab, and if absorbed into the blood, collapse and pulmonary oedema.

Destructive poisons: mercury and lead. Corrosive sublimate, that is mercuric chloride, is readily soluble in water. It forms albuminates with tissue proteins. When swallowed there is burning in the mouth, vomiting of blood, and then renal failure develops. In death from corrosive sublimate, diphtheritic inflammation of the large intestine, that is "sublimate dysentery", and an enlarged kidney with a thickened cortex, that is "sublimate kidney", are found. Organic mercury, granosan and mercusan, poisons chronically. The kidneys and intestine are less affected, there is no stomatitis, and encephalopathy is marked. Attention, risk of error: in lead, unlike mercury, the intestine and kidneys are less affected.

Arsenic and thallium poisoning. Pure arsenic is insoluble in water and fat, and on oxidation in air poisonous compounds form. Trivalent compounds are more poisonous than pentavalent. The lethal dose is 0.1–0.2 g. The gastrointestinal form develops on entry by mouth: metallic taste, vomiting, cholera-like diarrhoea. The paralytic form occurs with a large dose or parenteral administration and proceeds with encephalopathy and coma. Arsenic accumulates in the liver, skin, hair, nails and bone; this is cumulation. It persists in the corpse for years, so toxicological examination is decisive.

Case analysis: a heavy metal. A farmer's family consumed flour made from grain treated with granosan. After months one of them began to lose weight, with a metallic taste in the mouth, tremor of the hands and insomnia. Question: why may a wrong diagnosis be made in such a situation? Detecting poisoning with heavy metals may present difficulty and lead to diagnostic errors. Basis of diagnosis: a full history, clinical and morphological changes and the results of toxicological examination. The decisive importance lies in toxicological examination.

Blood poisons: carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide is formed in incomplete combustion, is colourless and odourless; it converts haemoglobin into carboxyhaemoglobin. Signs: headache, ringing in the ears, nausea, flushing of the face; then convulsive coma. Cadaveric lividity, muscles and liquid blood are pinkish-red; for confirmation, spectrophotometric quantitative examination is carried out. In normal blood, in the Hoppe-Seyler and Liebmann tests, a brown-black colour forms and one band is seen in the spectrum. In carbon-monoxide blood, in these tests the colour does not change and two bands are retained in the spectrum.

Methaemoglobin-forming poisons. The group includes nitrates and nitrites, nitrobenzene, aniline, Berthollet's salt, hydroquinone. Nitrates act only after being converted into nitrite in the intestine, so they are weaker than nitrite. Methaemoglobin is brown: trivalent iron is firmly bound to hydroxyl, so haemoglobin cannot carry oxygen. The first signs appear when methaemoglobin exceeds 30%, and death occurs when it exceeds 70%. Cadaveric lividity is bluish-brown. Attention: after 1–2 days methaemoglobin may not be found in the blood; in severe poisoning it is detected for 5–6 days.

CNS-paralysing poisons: cyanides. Potassium cyanide is a white substance readily soluble in water; hydrocyanic acid is a colourless, volatile liquid smelling of bitter almond. The cyanide anion binds iron in the cell respiratory enzyme cytochrome oxidase. Even when there is enough oxygen in the blood, tissue hypoxia develops. Amygdalin in the kernels of fresh fruits, that is apricot, peach and plum, forms hydrocyanic acid under the action of intestinal enzymes. On the corpse the lividity is cherry-reddish and a bitter almond smell comes from the cavities; because of its volatility it may quickly disappear.

Hydrogen sulphide and organophosphorus compounds. Hydrogen sulphide is a gas smelling of rotten eggs. Because it is heavier than air, it collects in mines and sewer pits. Poisoning is usually accidental. Hydrogen sulphide, like cyanides, binds iron in cytochrome oxidase and disturbs tissue respiration. It acts mainly on the nervous system. Organophosphorus compounds, that is OPCs, inhibit the enzyme cholinesterase. As a result acetylcholine accumulates in tissues and the cholinergic system is excited. The local action is weak.

Ethyl alcohol: toxicokinetics and diagnosis. The resorption, that is absorption, period is usually 1–2 hours; then the elimination period begins. In resorption the blood is higher and rising, the urine lower than the blood. In elimination the blood begins to fall, the urine is high. With repeated intake the blood rises again and the urine stays high. In the Rappoport test, if alcohol is present the pink colour of permanganate disappears; it detects even 0.3–0.4 per mille. Widmark's constant is the fall of alcohol in the blood per hour; if it cannot be determined, the average of 0.13–0.15 is taken.

t: Degrees of intoxication and alcohol surrogates
n: Degrees of intoxication and alcohol surrogates. In the blood, 0.5–1.5 per mille is mild, 1.5–2.5 moderate, 2.5–3.0 severe intoxication; above 3.0 is poisoning. Methanol is oxidised to formaldehyde and formic acid: acidosis, visual disturbance. The lethal dose of methanol is 30–100 ml, and there is a latent period. Ethylene glycol is converted to oxalic acid and damages the liver and kidneys; the lethal dose is 100–200 ml. With butyl alcohol the lethal dose is 200–250 ml, and a sweet smell comes from the internal organs. With amyl alcohol the lethal dose is 20–30 ml, with a smell of fusel oil. Higher alcohols damage the brain and kidneys.

Sleeping drugs and CNS-stimulating poisons. Barbiturates, that is veronal and nembutal, and tranquillisers depress the central nervous system. Clinical picture: deep sleep, fall in blood pressure, coma; death from paralysis of the respiratory centre. No characteristic changes are found on the corpse; there may be tablet remnants in the stomach. Because a therapeutic dose is possible, quantitative forensic chemical examination is necessary. Psychotonics, that is caffeine and phenamine, and antidepressants, that is imizine, stimulate the CNS. In a large dose psychosis arises, and with frequent intake, habituation and dependence.

Atropine, pilocarpine, clonidine, muscle relaxants. Atropine is an alkaloid of belladonna, thorn apple and henbane: flushing of the face, dilated pupils, delirium. The lethal dose is 0.1 g; it persists in the corpse for months, and forensic chemistry decides. Pilocarpine: profuse sweating and salivation, constricted pupils, bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema. The lethal dose is 0.06 g; on the corpse a constricted pupil and an abundance of mucus are noted. Clonidine is added to a drink: drowsiness, persistent fall in blood pressure, bradycardia, hypothermia. The lethal dose for adults is 0.005–0.01 g.

t: Classification of narcotics and drug-related death
n: Classification of narcotics and drug-related death. Substances are natural, semi-synthetic or synthetic; the action is sedative or stimulant. Natural ones include cannabis, morphine, codeine and cocaine. Semi-synthetic: heroin, mescaline, ephedrone. Synthetic: amphetamine, promedol, methadone, sombrevin. DRD, that is drug related death, means cases of death directly or indirectly related to use. DRD includes a large dose, the consequences of long-term intake, suicide, accident and homicide.

Opiates, cannabis and cocaine. Opiates act in 20–30 minutes by mouth and in 10–15 minutes under the skin; they accumulate more in the liver. Death from opiates occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre; morphine in the corpse is not broken down and is found even after months. In morphine the pupil is constricted, with cyanosis and coma; the lethal dose by mouth is 0.2–0.4 g, parenterally 0.1–0.2 g. With dry opium there is nausea, dyspnoea and stupor; by mouth 2–5 g. Cannabis is quickly broken down, the pupil is dilated, with nystagmus and tachycardia, and it usually ends without death. With cocaine there is excited euphoria and arrhythmia; death may occur from paralysis of the respiratory centre or from fibrillation.

Amphetamines, spice, precursors. Amphetamines are synthetic derivatives of phenylethylamine that stimulate the central nervous system; the action resembles cocaine, weaker but longer-lasting. "Ecstasy", that is MDMA, methylenedioxymethamphetamine, is a club tablet; the lethal dose is 500 mg. Spice is a mixture of plant material with a synthetic cannabinoid. Repeated intake gives mental dependence and tolerance; on stopping, an abstinence syndrome is seen. Habituation to opiates develops on average in 25–30 days. Precursors are substances used in making narcotics: acids, potassium permanganate, ethyl ether, acetone, toluene, piperidine, ergotamine and ephedrine.

Laboratory detection of narcotic substances. For cannabinoids, 10 ml of blood, 10 ml of urine, 10 ml of saliva and a wash from the fingers of the hands are taken. For other substances: 15–20 ml of blood and at least 200 ml of urine; materials are taken as soon as possible. If cannabis is suspected, the fingers are wiped with alcohol cotton wool, the alcohol is allowed to evaporate, and the swab is wrapped in a bag. In urine cannabinoids are detected after 1–3 hours and persist for 24–168 hours. Heroin after 2–6 hours, 24–72 hours; cocaine after 2–6 hours, 48–72 hours; phencyclidine after 4–6 hours, 7–14 days.

t: External examination and skin: injection marks
n: External examination and skin: injection marks. Drug addiction may be suspected already at external examination: emaciation 20.3%, obesity 9.4%, altered skin trophism, tattoos, destruction of teeth. Injection marks in 76.4%: usually in the cubital fossa and forearms; rarely on the palm, thigh, genital organ, tongue and neck. Old marks are "tracks" of small scars along the vein; fresh ones are punctate punctures with a dark-red crust. Sometimes there is no puncture, but small haemorrhages occur in characteristic places. The absence of signs does not exclude drug addiction. Histologically: fibrosis in the dermis, lymphoid-macrophage infiltrate, haemorrhages of different ages and haemosiderin; sometimes chronic panniculitis.

Brain changes: acute narcotic poisoning. In the brains of those dying of opiate overdose there is oedema and swelling: the dura is tense, the sulci and gyri flattened, the weight 1500–1850 g. The soft membrane is thin, transparent, its veins dilated and congested; sometimes Pacchionian granulations and fine punctate haemorrhages. On section, the brain substance is moist and glistening, and the ventricles are dilated and filled with clear fluid. Punctate haemorrhages are most frequent at the border of the medulla oblongata and pons and in the roof of the midbrain, and may be significant in thanatogenesis. In long-term use there is brain atrophy and fibrosis of the soft membrane, arachnofibrosis in about 90%; in the acute state, however, there is congestion of the membranes without oedema.

t: General asphyxial and characteristic signs: acute narcotic poisoning
n: General asphyxial and characteristic signs: acute narcotic poisoning. Liquid blood in the heart cavities in 100% of cases; small haemorrhages under the pleura and in the brain in only half. Constant signs: abundant, diffuse dark-violet cadaveric lividity, congestion of the soft membranes of the brain, cerebral oedema, subpleural haemorrhages. Cyanosis and puffiness of the face in only 12%; congestion of the conjunctivae of the eyes without ecchymoses is a difference from other asphyxias. Signs characteristic of a narcotic: congestion of the membranes without oedema; haemorrhage into the lung; large polymorphic subpleural haemorrhages and subepicardial haemorrhages along the base of the heart.

t: Lung: changes in acute narcotic poisoning
n: Lung: changes in acute narcotic poisoning. Macroscopically: massive oedema of the lungs in 84.9%, with frothy pink fluid flowing from the cut surface; haemorrhages of various shapes, including subpleural. In 27.4% of cases foci of peribronchial or subpleural pneumonia are found macroscopically, the cause being immunodeficiency and non-sterile injections. Histologically: alveolar and interstitial oedema, congestion, acute haemorrhages into the alveoli, erythrocyte stasis and sludge. Dystelectasis and uneven emphysema; regular, that is in 100%, focal haemosiderosis is distinguished by the Perls reaction from formalin pigment.

t: Four groups of changes in the corpse
n: Four groups of changes in the corpse. The changes found in a corpse in death associated with the use of narcotic substances are conventionally divided into four groups. The first is specific, neurochemical changes; they are insignificant for forensic practice, since only complex methods reveal them. The second is traces of repeated intake: ulcers on the vein, scars, granulomas. The third is injection infections: immunodeficiency, hepatitis. The fourth is lifestyle: emaciation, tuberculosis, tattoos. Attention: risk of error. These signs are indirect evidence, and a reliable conclusion is drawn only with forensic chemical confirmation.

Case analysis: suspected drug addiction. On a corpse, small ulcers and scars of different ages along a vein, emaciation, and a syringe-shaped tattoo on the skin were found. In addition: granulomas were found in the lungs, and hepatitis transmitted by injection is suspected. Question: relying on these signs, can it be concluded categorically that a narcotic substance was taken? Answer: no. The signs are indirect evidence; they are assessed together with the circumstances of the case, clinical data and mainly the forensic chemical results.

t: Importance of laboratory examinations and their errors
n: Importance of laboratory examinations and their errors. In a false positive result, a poison may be found even without poisoning. Cause: use of a drug, formation in putrefaction, occupational contact. Deficiencies in taking or examining the object may also lead to a false positive result. A false negative result occurs if the poison breaks down quickly, intensive infusion was given, much time has passed or a method of detection does not yet exist. Therefore forensic chemical results are always assessed together with other data.

Conclusion and key rules. Diagnosis relies on data collected in three stages: the scene, examination of the corpse and laboratory examinations. With functional poisons, characteristic changes are often not found on the corpse. Therefore medical documents, the clinical picture and laboratory results become the main evidence. Of the laboratory examinations, forensic chemical examination is carried out most often. It determines quality and quantity, and samples are taken by the "three points" rule. Attention: the result cannot be assessed in isolation. A poison may be found even without poisoning, that is a false positive, and in poisoning it may not be found.
